text: The long-term viability of adsorption-based treatment systems for PFAS-contaminated water depends not only on removal efficiency but also on how adsorbents are regenerated, managed and ultimately disposed of at the end of their service life. This review highlights that while notable progress has been made, no single regeneration method offers a universal solution. Thermal regeneration remains the most established approach, particularly for carbon-based adsorbents, but its high energy demand and potential structural damage con- strain its wider application. Solvent- and chemical-based methods achieve strong recovery and, in some cases, good multi-cycle stability, yet their benefits are offset by the generation of PFAS-contaminated liquid wastes requiring downstream treatment. Emerging electro- chemical and hybrid techniques show promise by combining desorption with partial in situ degradation, but their technical feasibility, durability and economic viability at scale remain uncertain. When regeneration is no longer viable, the disposal or destruction of PFAS- saturated adsorbents remains challenging. High-temperature incineration is currently the most reliable route for near-complete PFAS mineralisation but is limited by cost, energy de- mand and the risk of incomplete destruction. Alternative oxidative or chemical destruction approaches are under development but have yet to demonstrate large-scale performance, and immobilisation and stabilisation techniques offer only interim containment rather than permanent elimination.

These materials are highly compatible with solvent and mild chemical regeneration, which can Water 2025, 17, 2813 10 of 28 efficiently desorb PFASs without damaging the matrix. Typical methods include methanol, ethanol, and mixed solvent systems such as methanol plus NaCl or alkaline brines, often achieving more than 90% desorption over several cycles [29,100–103]. Multi-cycle studies demonstrate that such mild solvent systems combined with moderate ionic strength offer the most viable pathways for long-term use [29,104]. In contrast, polymeric matrices are inherently susceptible to degradation under high-temperature or oxidative conditions, and thermal regeneration is rarely applied because it can cause irreversible changes in resin structure and loss of functional groups [98,105]. Some emerging oxidative hybrid methods can partially regenerate polymeric sorbents by coupling solvent washing with mild oxi- dants, but these approaches risk damaging the polymer backbone or functional sites over repeated cycles and remain at an experimental stage [106,107]. Overall, polymeric PFAS adsorbents exhibit a favourable balance of high capacity, tuneable chemistry and gentle regeneration potential, but their heat and oxidant sensitivity necessitate careful choice of regenerant conditions to preserve long-term performance.

T echnological innov a tions in PF AS adsorption The persistent nature and widespread occurrence of PFASs in water systems have exposed the limitations of conventional treatment methods and catalysed a wave of innovations in adsorption-based technologies. Recent advances in material science, process engineering and systems integration are driv - ing the development of novel adsorption platforms that not only enhance PFAS removal efficiency but also prioritise sustainability, scalability and cost-effectiveness. This section highlights five key areas of technological advancement in PFAS adsorption. Membra ne-based adsorption s ys tems Membrane-based adsorption technologies represent a prom - ising convergence of separation and adsorption processes. These systems incorporate functional adsorbents such as AC, CNTs, MOFs and ion-exchange resins into porous mem - branes, enabling simultaneous filtration and contaminant capture (Davoodbeygi et al. 2023). Owing to their high surface area and customisable pore structures, adsorptive membranes can effectively target both long- and short-chain PFASs, which are often inadequately removed by traditional techniques. Advanced hybrid membranes, including those functiona - lised with zwitterionic polymers or thin-film composites, offer enhanced selectivity by leveraging electrostatic, hydro - phobic and hydrogen bonding interactions (Gu et al. 2024). Zwitterionic electrospun membranes, for example, have demonstrated strong PFAS adsorption capacity while resist - ing fouling in complex matrices.

text: Conclusions In this study, the performance of a hybrid UF – RO system for the removal of PFAS from real TWW was investigated, focusing on removal performance, fouling behavior, and the role of water matrix constitu - ents. The results show that the combined UF – RO treatment significantly reduced PFAS concentrations by 95.9 %. Ultrafiltration contributed to PFAS rejection (60 %-84 %) through mechanisms such as size exclusion, dynamic fouling layer creation, and electrostatic repulsion. High sulfate concentrations affected the mem - brane surface charge and possiblyy enhanced PFAS retention, while chlorides played a lesser role but possibly affected the local ionic con - ditions at the membrane interface. Due to the much smaller pore size RO, the concentration of all detected PFAS dropped below the LOQ, i.e., they were almost completely rejected. In addition to the concentration-based removal, the reduction in PFAS mass loading was also quantified in this study. The system used is able to reduce approximately 3.5 g of PFAS per year, of which 2667.3 mg with the UF, and 825.2 mg with the RO. These results underline not only the technical effectiveness of the UF – RO system, but also its importance for the environment, as signifi - cant amounts of PFAS can be rejected before they reach natural aquifers.

Membrane separation processes are widely applied in water/waste - water treatment and industries and it was found to be effective in rejecting short and long chain PFAS with efficiencies exceeding 90 % [ 24 , 25 ]. Generally, in membrane separation systems, feed water con - taining PFAS molecules is rejected by the membrane (semi-permeable selective barrier) while water molecules are passing to the permeation side of the system. The most famous, effective and largely investigated membrane systems for PFAS removal are pressure driven membrane systems, particularly nanofiltration (NF) and reverse osmosis (RO) sys - tems. The defined removal mechanism are size exclusion, electrostatic repulsion and solution diffusion for NF and RO, respectively. The effi - ciency of these membranes in rejecting PFASs from aqueous environ - ments were reported to approach 99 % [ 26 , 27 ]. The majority of studies on the rejection of PFAS by RO and NF have relied on bench scale systems, which may not represent the performance of pilot- and full scale-scale systems [ 45 , 46 ] due to leaking, concentra - tion polarization [ 47 ], and operating in dead-end filtration instead of crossflow [ 48 ]. Many studies have used deionized or tap water spiked with AFFF or single PFAS solutes [ 41 ], focusing on PFAAs, which omits the multitude of PFAA precursors that can occur at sites historically impacted by AFFF use [ 16 – 18 , 24 , 50 , 51 ].
